name: Joint Hypermobility Syndrome

ethnicAssociations: Higher prevalence in Asian and African populations
More common in populations with greater baseline flexibility

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: Brighton Criteria (1998) / Hypermobility Spectrum Disorder Framework (2017)

criteria.description: Arthralgia in 1-3 joints or back pain, spondylosis, spondylolysis
Dislocation or subluxation in more than one joint or one joint on more than one occasion
Three or more soft tissue lesions (epicondylitis, tenosynovitis, bursitis)
Skin abnormalities: striae, hyperextensibility, thin skin, papyraceous scarring
Eye signs: drooping eyelids, myopia, antimongoloid slant
Varicose veins, hernia, or uterine/rectal prolapse

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Brighton criteria: 2 major, OR 1 major + 2 minor, OR 4 minor, OR 2 minor + unequivocally affected first-degree relative. Since 2017, patients not meeting full hEDS criteria may be classified under the Hypermobility Spectrum Disorder (HSD) framework.
diagnosticCriteria.notes: The relationship between JHS and hEDS remains debated. The 2017 EDS classification introduced the HSD framework to capture patients who are symptomatic from hypermobility but do not meet hEDS criteria.

pathognomonic.symptomName: Generalized joint hypermobility with associated musculoskeletal symptoms
pathognomonic.notes: Hypermobility is the defining feature when accompanied by symptoms
searchTerms: overall loose joints with muscle pain
soft tissue injuries like tendon inflammation
poor balance and body position sense

imaging: Radiographs may show no structural abnormality
MRI may show soft tissue injuries disproportionate to mechanism
Ultrasound may identify tendinopathy or effusion
genetic: Genetic testing primarily used to exclude heritable CTDs (EDS subtypes, Marfan)
other: Upper limb and lower limb hypermobility questionnaire (5-part questionnaire)

distinguishingFeatures: hEDS meets more stringent 2017 diagnostic criteria
hEDS has more prominent systemic features (>= 5 of 12)
JHS/HSD may represent milder part of same spectrum
Fibromyalgia does not require joint hypermobility
Marfan has aortic root dilation and ectopia lentis
Marfan has tall stature with arachnodactyly

redFlags: Significant skin fragility or atrophic scarring (consider EDS subtypes)
Vascular events at young age (consider vascular EDS)
Progressive aortic root dilation (consider Marfan or LDS)
Bone fragility or blue sclerae (consider osteogenesis imperfecta)
references: Grahame R, Bird HA, Child A. The revised (Brighton 1998) criteria for the diagnosis of benign joint hypermobility syndrome (BJHS). J Rheumatol. 2000;27(7):1777-9.
Castori M, et al. A framework for the classification of joint hypermobility and related conditions. Am J Med Genet C Semin Med Genet. 2017;175(1):148-57.
Hakim A, Grahame R. Joint hypermobility. Best Pract Res Clin Rheumatol. 2003;17(6):989-1004.
